entities.name: Saint Aurelia’s Church, Strasbourg
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Saint Aurelia's Church (Église Sainte-Aurélie, German: Sankt-Aureliuskirche) in Strasbourg is a significant Evangelical Lutheran church in the city — one of Strasbourg's historic Reformation-era Protestant churches — dedicated to Saint Aurelia of Strasbourg, a 3rd-century Christian martyr who, according to hagiographic tradition, was one of the companions of Saint Ursula and the 11,000 virgins martyred at Cologne, and whose relics were brought to Strasbourg making her the city's principal early Christian martyr.

Saint Aurelia was the patron saint of Strasbourg before the Reformation, and her church was one of the city's principal pre-Reformation Catholic churches that was subsequently converted to Protestant use during Strasbourg's Reformation under Martin Bucer (1520s-1530s). The conversion of Strasbourg's Catholic churches to Protestant use is one of the key processes of the urban Reformation — as Protestant civic majorities gained control of city governments across the Holy Roman Empire, they took over church buildings, removed 'idolatrous' images and altars, and adapted the spaces to Reformed worship.

Saint Aurelia's church thus embodies the transition from Catholic to Lutheran Strasbourg — the relics of the city's patron martyr contained in a church now serving a community that rejected the cult of relics and saints. This theological paradox is characteristic of the Reformation's complex relationship to the sacred geography it inherited. The church is part of Strasbourg's extraordinary collection of historic religious buildings that together document the city's medieval Catholic, Reformation Protestant, and Franco-German heritage.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Saint Aurelia's Church Strasbourg — dedicated to the city's patron martyr, converted from Catholic to Protestant use during Bucer's Reformation, and embodying the paradox of Protestant worship in an early Christian martyr shrine — is historically significant as a monument of the urban Reformation's transformation of Catholic sacred geography.
